Lesson 0002  /  HFT Trading Practice Repo

Crossing the Python/C++ Boundary
for Numeric Aggregation over Time Series

How volume_metrics.cpp, bindings.cpp, and fetch_eia() work together — from EIA API to C++ vector to Python list — and all the boundary decisions in between.

Contents

  1. When to move computation to C++
  2. pybind11 type system: std::vector<double> ↔ Python list
  3. NaN handling across the boundary
  4. The parity test pattern
  5. EIA v2 API: paginated JSON and the cache→charge→save flow
  6. The APIBudget pattern
  7. Non-positive value filtering
  8. Return type conventions: same-length output, NaN for invalid positions

1. When to Move Computation to C++

Python is expressive and fast to iterate on, but three concrete bottlenecks push inner-loop numeric work into C++:

  • Tight loops over time series. Python executes each iteration as bytecode dispatch with reference-count bookkeeping. For a 10 000-week EIA storage history, a loop over list[float] is 20–50× slower than the equivalent compiled loop over double*.
  • Cache locality. A C++ std::vector<double> is a contiguous slab of 8-byte values. Python list is an array of pointers to heap-allocated PyFloatObjects (56 bytes each, scattered in memory). The C++ layout fits more elements in an L1 cache line and avoids pointer chasing.
  • No GIL during compute. A C extension can release the Global Interpreter Lock (py::gil_scoped_release) and run on a background thread without serialising through the interpreter. Pure Python code cannot do this.

The Python equivalent vs the C++ loop

The Python reference implementation for capacity_utilization is a straightforward list comprehension:

Python reference (tests/test_oil_volume.py)
def _py_capacity_utilization(storage_kb, capacity_kb):
    import math
    return [
        math.nan if math.isnan(s) else s / capacity_kb * 100.0
        for s in storage_kb
    ]

The C++ version does exactly the same computation, but iterates over a contiguous buffer with no Python object overhead:

cpp/oil_volume/volume_metrics.cpp
std::vector<double> capacity_utilization(
    const std::vector<double>& storage_kb, double capacity_kb)
{
    if (capacity_kb <= 0.0)
        throw std::invalid_argument("capacity_kb must be positive");
    std::vector<double> out(storage_kb.size());
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < storage_kb.size(); ++i) {
        out[i] = std::isnan(storage_kb[i])
            ? NaN
            : (storage_kb[i] / capacity_kb * 100.0);
    }
    return out;
}

The compiler auto-vectorises this loop on -O3 -march=native, processing four doubles per cycle with AVX2 instructions. The Python version cannot benefit from SIMD.

Rule of thumb Move to C++ when: (1) the loop runs over more than ~1 000 elements, (2) the per-element operation is arithmetic rather than IO, and (3) the function will be called on every bar or tick. The EIA storage metrics meet all three criteria.

2. pybind11 Type System: std::vector<double> ↔ Python list

When Python calls oil_volume_cpp.capacity_utilization([30000.0, 45000.0], 76000.0), pybind11's type caster system converts types at the boundary before the C++ function ever sees them.

The critical include

cpp/oil_volume/bindings.cpp
#include <pybind11/pybind11.h>
#include <pybind11/stl.h>    // enables std::vector<double> ↔ list[float]

#include "volume_metrics.hpp"

namespace py = pybind11;
using namespace oil_volume;

PYBIND11_MODULE(oil_volume_cpp, m) {
    m.doc() = "C++ core for oil-volume metrics (pybind11 bridge)";

    m.def("capacity_utilization", &capacity_utilization,
        py::arg("storage_kb"), py::arg("capacity_kb"), "...");

    m.def("days_of_supply", &days_of_supply,
        py::arg("storage_kb"), py::arg("production_kbd"), "...");

    m.def("fill_rate", &fill_rate,
        py::arg("storage_kb"), "...");
}
Missing <pybind11/stl.h> is a compile error Without #include <pybind11/stl.h>, the compiler cannot find a type caster for std::vector<double> and will produce a cryptic template error. It does not fall back silently.

What py::arg does

py::arg("storage_kb") attaches a keyword-argument name to the C++ parameter. Without it, Python callers must use positional arguments only. With it, both of these are valid:

# positional
cpp.capacity_utilization([30000.0], 76000.0)

# keyword
cpp.capacity_utilization(storage_kb=[30000.0], capacity_kb=76000.0)

The conversion pipeline

DirectionPython typeC++ typeCost
Call (in)list[float]std::vector<double>One allocation + element copy
Return (out)list[float]std::vector<double>Move out of C++, then copy to Python list
Scalar (in)float or intdoubleZero allocation
ErrorValueErrorstd::invalid_argumentpybind11 re-raises automatically

The conversion is not zero-copy: pybind11 allocates a new std::vector on the way in and a new Python list on the way out. For HFT hot paths, pass NumPy arrays directly (via #include <pybind11/numpy.h>) to work on shared memory. For weekly EIA data (52 elements/year), the copy cost is negligible.

3. NaN Handling Across the Boundary

IEEE 754 NaN ("Not a Number") propagates through both languages, but the API for producing and testing it differs between C++ and Python.

Producing NaN in C++

cpp/oil_volume/volume_metrics.cpp
static constexpr double NaN = std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN();

quiet_NaN() produces a "quiet" NaN — one that propagates through arithmetic without raising a floating-point exception. (A "signalling" NaN raises SIGFPE on first use; never use it for sentinel values.)

Testing NaN in C++ and Python

LanguageTestWhy not x == NaN
C++std::isnan(x)IEEE 754: NaN != NaN is always true
Pythonmath.isnan(x)Same reason; float('nan') == float('nan') is False

NaN propagation in days_of_supply

cpp/oil_volume/volume_metrics.cpp
std::vector<double> days_of_supply(
    const std::vector<double>& storage_kb,
    const std::vector<double>& production_kbd)
{
    // length guard — mismatch is a programmer error, not a data issue
    if (storage_kb.size() != production_kbd.size())
        throw std::invalid_argument(
            "storage_kb and production_kbd must be the same length");

    std::vector<double> out(storage_kb.size());
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < storage_kb.size(); ++i) {
        if (std::isnan(storage_kb[i])
         || std::isnan(production_kbd[i])
         || production_kbd[i] <= 0.0) {
            out[i] = NaN;           // explicit propagation
        } else {
            out[i] = storage_kb[i] / production_kbd[i];
        }
    }
    return out;
}

Three conditions all produce NaN output: either input is NaN, or production is non-positive. This is the correct defensive pattern: arithmetic on NaN produces NaN anyway, but the non-positive guard prevents a division-by-zero or a semantically nonsensical negative days-of-supply value.

NaN propagation diagram

Input (Python list[float]) [30000.0, NaN, 60000.0, 0.0 ] ← storage_kb [100.0, 200.0, NaN, 300.0] ← production_kbd (0.0 treated as invalid) │ │ pybind11 copies to std::vector<double> ▼ C++ loop (days_of_supply) i=0: 30000/100 = 300.0 ← valid i=1: isnan(storage[1]) → NaN ← NaN in, NaN out i=2: isnan(production[2]) → NaN ← NaN in, NaN out i=3: production <= 0 → NaN ← non-positive guard │ │ pybind11 copies to Python list[float] ▼ Output (Python list[float]) [300.0, NaN, NaN, NaN] math.isnan(result[1]) → True ← Python correctly sees NaN

4. The Parity Test Pattern

A parity test compares a C++ result against an independent Python reference implementation and asserts they agree within floating-point tolerance. It serves as both a correctness gate and a regression guard.

The _close() helper

tests/test_oil_volume.py
def _close(a, b, tol=1e-9):
    if math.isnan(a) and math.isnan(b):
        return True          # NaN == NaN in this context
    if math.isnan(a) or math.isnan(b):
        return False         # one NaN, one real number — mismatch
    return abs(a - b) < tol

The helper has three cases: both NaN (equal), one NaN (unequal), or both finite (within tolerance). This handles the IEEE 754 problem where NaN != NaN by convention — in a parity test, if both sides agree on "no data here", that is a successful match.

A complete parity test

tests/test_oil_volume.py
def test_capacity_utilization_parity(cpp):
    storage = [30000.0, 45000.0, 60000.0, 75000.0]
    cap = 76000.0

    got      = cpp.capacity_utilization(storage, cap)
    expected = _py_capacity_utilization(storage, cap)

    assert all(_close(g, e) for g, e in zip(got, expected))

Parity test structure

same input │ ┌───────────┴───────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ C++ path Python reference cpp.capacity_utilization() _py_capacity_utilization() │ │ │ pybind11 boundary │ pure Python list comp ▼ ▼ list[float] list[float] │ │ └───────────┬───────────┘ ▼ _close(g, e, tol=1e-9) for every element pair │ ┌────────┴────────┐ │ │ PASS FAIL both match logic diverged (or both NaN) or NaN mismatch
Tolerance choice 1e-9 is tight enough to catch logic errors but loose enough to tolerate different floating-point evaluation orders between C++ (which may use FMA instructions) and Python. For integer-valued inputs the result is exact and a tighter tolerance like 1e-12 is appropriate.
The fixture pattern The cpp fixture calls pytest.skip() rather than pytest.fail() when the extension is not built. A missing extension is a configuration problem, not a code bug — so the rest of the test suite keeps running.

5. EIA v2 API: Paginated JSON and the Cache→Charge→Save Flow

The U.S. Energy Information Administration's v2 API returns results in pages of up to 5 000 rows. A single EIA crude storage series (weekly since 1982) has more than 2 000 rows, so the client must loop until the page returns fewer rows than the page size.

Series ID format

EIA series IDs encode product, geography, and frequency. PET.WCSSTUS1.W decodes as:

SegmentMeaning
PETPetroleum category
WCSSTUS1Weekly Cushing OK crude stock, US
WWeekly frequency

The pagination loop

src/oil_alpha/sources.py — fetch_eia() inner _fetch()
rows = []
offset = 0
page_size = 5000
while True:
    params = urllib.parse.urlencode({
        "api_key": key, "start": start, "end": end,
        "sort[0][column]": "period", "sort[0][direction]": "asc",
        "offset": offset, "length": page_size,
    })
    url = f"https://api.eia.gov/v2/seriesid/{series_id}?{params}"
    with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=30) as resp:
        payload = json.loads(resp.read().decode("utf-8"))
    data = payload.get("response", {}).get("data", [])
    if not data:
        break
    rows.extend(data)
    if len(data) < page_size:  # last page — fewer rows than page_size
        break
    offset += page_size

The data flow end to end

EIA API https://api.eia.gov/v2/seriesid/PET.WCSSTUS1.W?... │ │ HTTP GET, possibly multiple pages (offset += 5000) ▼ Paginated JSON {"response": {"data": [{period, value, ...}, ...]}} │ │ json.loads() + pd.DataFrame(rows) ▼ DataFrame columns: period (str), value (float), unit, ... │ │ df["value"] > 0 filter, pd.to_numeric coerce ▼ Cleaned DataFrame saved to disk cache (parquet or csv) │ │ df["value"].tolist() ▼ list[float] Python list, one element per week │ │ pybind11 boundary — cpp.fill_rate(storage_kb) ▼ std::vector<double> contiguous 8-byte array in C++ heap │ │ volume_metrics loop ▼ std::vector<double> result │ │ pybind11 boundary — copy to Python ▼ list[float] same length as input, NaN where invalid

6. The APIBudget Pattern

An APIBudget tracks network calls by source so that tests and production code can assert that caching is working — a cache hit should never increment the usage counter.

Charge only on network hit

src/oil_alpha/sources.py — _from_cache_or()
def _from_cache_or(kind, symbol, start, end, fetch, *, budget, source, use_cache):
    if use_cache:
        cached = cache.load(kind, symbol, start, end)
        if cached is not None and not cached.empty:
            return cached          # cache hit: no charge, return immediately

    df = fetch()                   # network hit: calls the HTTP round-trip
    budget.charge(source)          # charged ONLY after successful network fetch
    if use_cache and not df.empty:
        cache.save(df, kind, symbol, start, end)
    return df

The cache check happens before any network I/O. If the cache returns a non-empty DataFrame, the function returns immediately and budget.charge() is never called. This makes the invariant easy to test:

The caching assertion

tests/test_oil_volume.py
def test_fetch_eia_caches_on_second_call(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    # ... setup fake cache with pre-populated data ...
    budget = APIBudget()

    result = fetch_eia(
        "PET.WCSSTUS1.W", "2023-01-01", "2023-01-31",
        budget=budget, use_cache=True, api_key="test-key"
    )

    eia_usage = budget.usage.get("eia")
    assert eia_usage is None or eia_usage.used == 0  # cache hit = free

Budget charge flow

fetch_eia("PET.WCSSTUS1.W", ...) │ ▼ _from_cache_or(...) │ ├─── cache.load() ──▶ hit (not None and not empty) │ │ │ └──▶ return cached ← budget.charge() SKIPPED │ └─── cache.load() ──▶ miss (None or empty) │ ▼ _fetch() ── HTTP GET ──▶ EIA API │ ▼ budget.charge("eia") ← counted here │ ▼ cache.save(df, ...) │ ▼ return df

7. Non-Positive Value Filtering

Oil storage values must be strictly positive — zero or negative values in the EIA response indicate missing data, reporting errors, or API artefacts. The filter is applied at both the Python ingestion layer and the C++ computation layer, for defence in depth.

Python ingestion filter

src/oil_alpha/sources.py — fetch_eia()
df["value"] = pd.to_numeric(df["value"], errors="coerce")
df = df[df["value"] > 0].copy()   # drop NaN, zero, and negative rows

pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce") first converts the JSON string "value" field to a float, coercing non-numeric strings to NaN. The subsequent > 0 filter drops both those NaN rows and any non-positive numerics in a single step.

C++ computation guard

cpp/oil_volume/volume_metrics.cpp — days_of_supply()
if (std::isnan(storage_kb[i])
 || std::isnan(production_kbd[i])
 || production_kbd[i] <= 0.0) {   // <= 0 guard here
    out[i] = NaN;
}

Even if clean data is guaranteed from the Python side, the C++ guard prevents a division-by-zero and ensures the output is always semantically meaningful. A days-of-supply value computed against zero or negative production would be infinite or negative — both are nonsensical for a trading signal.

Why filter in both places? The Python filter removes bad rows from storage. The C++ guard handles NaN values that can arise from other computation paths (e.g., a fill_rate output fed into days_of_supply) — not just from the raw EIA data. Each layer catches what the other cannot.

8. Return Type Conventions: Same-Length Output, NaN for Invalid Positions

All four C++ metric functions share the same output contract: the returned vector is always exactly the same length as the input, and positions that cannot produce a meaningful value are filled with NaN rather than being dropped or signalled with a special integer sentinel.

Why same-length output?

  • Alignment with the time axis. If the caller has a DataFrame with a period column, they can assign the result directly as a new column without reindexing.
  • Composability. Downstream functions can safely zip two outputs from the same input without length-mismatch errors.
  • Explicit invalidity. NaN is a first-class float value. A downstream chart or signal engine can test math.isnan(v) to skip invalid positions without needing a parallel boolean mask array.

fill_rate: the canonical example

fill_rate is the week-over-week change in storage. By definition, the first element has no prior period — there is nothing to subtract from. The output is initialised entirely to NaN, then filled from index 1 onward:

cpp/oil_volume/volume_metrics.cpp
std::vector<double> fill_rate(const std::vector<double>& storage_kb) {
    const std::size_t n = storage_kb.size();
    std::vector<double> out(n, NaN);   // ALL elements initialised to NaN

    for (std::size_t i = 1; i < n; ++i) {   // start at 1, not 0
        if (std::isnan(storage_kb[i]) || std::isnan(storage_kb[i - 1])) {
            out[i] = NaN;          // NaN input propagates
        } else {
            out[i] = storage_kb[i] - storage_kb[i - 1];
        }
    }
    return out;   // out[0] is always NaN — never touched by the loop
}

Output layout across all four functions

FunctionNaN positionsReason
capacity_utilizationWhere storage_kb[i] is NaNInvalid input propagated
days_of_supplyWhere either input is NaN or production ≤ 0NaN propagation + non-positive guard
fill_rateIndex 0 always; index i where either of its two inputs is NaNNo prior period at index 0
rolling_meanIndices 0 … window−2Window not yet full
fill_rate example Input: [400, 420, NaN, 410, 430] Init: [NaN, NaN, NaN, NaN, NaN] ← std::vector<double> out(n, NaN) Loop i=1: 420-400 = 20 → out[1] = 20 Loop i=2: isnan(NaN) → out[2] = NaN Loop i=3: isnan(prev NaN) → out[3] = NaN Loop i=4: 430-410 = 20 → out[4] = 20 Output: [NaN, 20, NaN, NaN, 20] ^ ^ ^ always NaN propagated NaN (gap in input)
HPP declaration review The header volume_metrics.hpp declares all four functions inside the oil_volume namespace. The bindings.cpp file uses using namespace oil_volume so that the m.def calls can reference capacity_utilization without the namespace prefix — matching the Python-facing name exactly.
cpp/oil_volume/volume_metrics.hpp
#pragma once
#include <vector>
#include <cstddef>
#include <limits>

namespace oil_volume {
std::vector<double> capacity_utilization(const std::vector<double>& storage_kb, double capacity_kb);
std::vector<double> days_of_supply(const std::vector<double>& storage_kb, const std::vector<double>& production_kbd);
std::vector<double> fill_rate(const std::vector<double>& storage_kb);
std::vector<double> rolling_mean(const std::vector<double>& values, int window);
}
